I'm setting up OpenVPN, but I'm a little cautious about opening ports, and "hardening" the machine with OpenVPN. I'd want it a little more like an appliance, if at all possible. My ISP doesn't seem to change my External IP very often, maybe once a year if that.

Edit: So, while Voat was being upgraded, I found a few options, but nothing concrete:

I could in theory use reverse SSH, but I'd need to find a relay I could trust to be in the middle.

My other thought would be be to use a "PogoPlug", install Arch/OpenPono+OpenVPN and hope that PogoPlug's servers can somehow, securely sit in the middle for a handshake.

I thought of something through Telegram or Pidgin Off-the-Record, but I can't find anything saying that could work either.

Edit edit: I think I figured a way to do it. I get a hosted box of some sort, likely a SeedBox that allows SSH. I setup DropBox or PushBullet, or SpiderOak (for open source). I drop a file on it saying "connect", and it connects to said SeedBox with reverse SSH. I then SSH in to the SeedBox and reverse to my home. Not perfect, but if anyone can think of a better way, I'm still all ears.

Ok, here's my analogy, I think it's brilliant, but you have to like Kung-Fu

Bruce Lee said, do not fear the man who knows 10,000 kicks, fear the man who has practiced one kick 10,000 times.

I don't think the kid that knows 15 ways to solve different fractions is going to go very far...I think the kid that knows 1 way to solve ALL fractions is going to go far in STEM.

To put this another way, Common Core is like Cobra Kahn, while traditional methods are like Mr. Miyagi. The Cobra Kahn guys learned all these different ways to fight and just did strength training...Mr. Miyagi taught the Karate Kid wax on / wax off, which made no damn sense at all...until the scene...Because the Karate Kid had practiced the same technique over and over and over, he suddenly had a very powerful understanding of the core concepts of karate...that core understanding is what led him to the creative skill to apply the crane kick in the last scene.

That's like traditional math (Miyagi's method) vs Common Core (the Kahn method). The kids learning common core learn tricks for specific situations, but never get mastery of the core math concepts. The traditionalists force you to drill on one technique until you know it inside and out before moving on to harder lessons. Because you know those core lessons so well, it's easier to apply to an unknown situation (i.e. the Crane Kick, or in other words, real world problems).
